title: Paediatric and Sports Physiotherapy
description: Child development and paediatric physiotherapy assessment, management of cerebral palsy and other childhood conditions, and sports injury prevention, assessment and rehabilitation.

topics.title: Paediatric Assessment and Development
topics.summary: Motor development, primitive reflexes, paediatric assessment tools and family-centred care.

notes.b: Typical motor milestones: head control (3–4 months), rolling (4–6 months), sitting unsupported (6–8 months), crawling (8–10 months), pulling to stand (9–10 months), walking independently (12–15 months), running (18 months), jumping with both feet (2 years), hopping on one foot (4 years). Development proceeds cephalocaudally and proximodistally. Primitive reflexes (Moro, asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR), palmar grasp, rooting, stepping) are present at birth and integrate by about 4–6 months; persistence suggests neurological impairment (e.g. cerebral palsy). Postural reactions (righting, equilibrium, protective/parachute reactions) emerge and support motor control. Red flags: persistent primitive reflexes, asymmetry, abnormal tone, hand preference before 12–18 months (suggests hemiplegia), not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months, and loss of skills.

Paediatric physiotherapy assessment includes birth history (prematurity, birth asphyxia, neonatal jaundice — common causes of neurodisability in Nigeria), developmental history, observation during play, tone (Modified Ashworth, Tardieu scale), range of movement (contractures), strength, posture, balance, gait, and function. Standardised tools: Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM-66/88) and Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) for cerebral palsy, Alberta Infant Motor Scale (AIMS), Peabody Developmental Motor Scales, and the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination (HINE) for early detection. The ICF framework (body structure/function, activity, participation, environmental and personal factors) guides goal setting. Family-centred care recognises parents as experts and partners: set goals with the family, teach home programmes, and address beliefs (some families attribute disability to spiritual causes, delaying care) and practical barriers (cost, transport, stigma, school access).

topics.title: Paediatric Neurological Conditions
topics.summary: Cerebral palsy management, spina bifida, Down syndrome, Erb's palsy and developmental delay.

notes.b: Cerebral palsy (CP) management is goal-directed, functional and family-centred: task-specific training and motor learning, strengthening (children with CP can safely strengthen), stretching and positioning to prevent contractures (standing frames, sleeping systems), orthoses (ankle–foot orthoses for equinus), mobility aids (walkers, wheelchairs), constraint-induced movement therapy and bimanual training for hemiplegia, hippotherapy and hydrotherapy where available, and management of spasticity (botulinum toxin injections followed by stretching and casting; baclofen; selective dorsal rhizotomy in specialised centres). Hip surveillance (regular hip X-rays in GMFCS III–V) prevents hip dislocation. Associated problems — epilepsy, feeding and nutrition, communication, vision and hearing, and learning difficulties — require multidisciplinary care. In Nigeria, community-based programmes and parent training (e.g. using locally made equipment — bamboo standing frames, adapted chairs) extend services.

Spina bifida (myelomeningocele): lower limb weakness and sensory loss by lesion level, hydrocephalus, bladder and bowel dysfunction, and orthopaedic deformities (clubfoot, hip dislocation, scoliosis); physiotherapy addresses mobility (orthoses, walking aids, wheelchairs), skin protection (insensate areas — pressure ulcers and burns), strengthening and family education; folic acid prevents neural tube defects. Down syndrome: hypotonia, ligamentous laxity, delayed motor milestones — encourage motor development through play, strengthening and balance; screen for atlantoaxial instability before contact sports. Obstetric brachial plexus palsy (Erb's palsy — C5–C6; 'waiter's tip' posture; common after difficult deliveries with shoulder dystocia): gentle range of movement, positioning, avoid traction on the arm, and splinting; most recover spontaneously within months, but those without biceps recovery by 3–6 months need surgical referral. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: progressive proximal weakness in boys (Gowers' sign) — maintain function and range, avoid over-fatigue, respiratory care and night splints.

topics.title: Paediatric Musculoskeletal and Respiratory Conditions
topics.summary: Clubfoot (Ponseti), torticollis, DDH, scoliosis, juvenile arthritis and paediatric respiratory care.

notes.b: Congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot — cavus, adductus, varus and equinus) is common in Nigeria; the Ponseti method (serial manipulation and long-leg casting weekly, percutaneous Achilles tenotomy in most cases, then foot abduction brace — 23 hours/day for 3 months, then night-time until about 4 years) has excellent outcomes and is delivered by trained physiotherapists and orthopaedic teams; adherence to bracing prevents relapse. Congenital muscular torticollis (sternocleidomastoid tightness — head tilted to the same side, rotated to the opposite side; plagiocephaly): stretching, positioning and handling advice. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH): screening (Ortolani, Barlow), ultrasound, Pavlik harness in infants; avoid tight swaddling with hips extended. Idiopathic scoliosis (adolescent girls): Adam's forward bend test, Cobb angle; bracing (20–40°), Schroth-based exercises, and surgery for severe curves. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: maintain range and strength, joint protection and splints. Blount's disease and rickets cause bowed legs in some Nigerian children.

Paediatric respiratory physiotherapy: bronchiolitis and uncomplicated pneumonia do not routinely need chest physiotherapy (no benefit shown); physiotherapy may help children with lobar collapse, excessive secretions, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis (rare in Africa), neuromuscular weakness, and ventilated children in ICU. Techniques adapted for children: positioning, modified postural drainage (avoid head-down in infants with reflux or raised ICP), percussion and vibrations (gentle, over clothing), assisted coughing, play-based breathing exercises (bubbles, blowing games), incentive spirometry and airway suctioning with care. Asthma education (inhaler with spacer and mask for young children, recognising triggers — dust, smoke, harmattan), exercise participation and breathing control. Children with sickle cell disease benefit from incentive spirometry during painful crises to prevent acute chest syndrome.

topics.title: Sports Injury Prevention and Assessment
topics.summary: Pre-participation screening, injury mechanisms, on-field management, and concussion.

notes.b: Sports physiotherapists work with athletes in football (the most popular sport in Nigeria), athletics, basketball, boxing, wrestling and para-sports. Injury prevention: pre-participation examination (medical history, cardiovascular screening — family history of sudden death, syncope, murmurs; ECG in some settings to detect hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; sickle cell trait awareness — exertional collapse with extreme exertion, heat and dehydration), musculoskeletal screening (flexibility, strength imbalances, previous injury — the strongest predictor of future injury), structured warm-up programmes (FIFA 11+ reduces injuries by about 30–50% in football), load management (avoid sudden spikes in training load — acute:chronic workload ratio), adequate recovery and sleep, appropriate equipment (footwear, shin guards, mouthguards) and playing surfaces, heat illness prevention (hydration, acclimatisation, scheduling in cooler times), and nutrition.

Pitch-side care: a systematic approach (DRSABCD — Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation); sudden cardiac arrest in athletes requires immediate CPR and AED use. Suspected spinal injury: in-line immobilisation and log roll, spinal board. Acute soft-tissue injuries: PEACE & LOVE principles. Sport-related concussion: a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head or body transmitting force to the head — signs include loss of consciousness (not required), confusion, balance problems, headache, dizziness, memory loss and visual disturbance. 'If in doubt, sit them out': remove from play, do not return the same day, assess with tools such as SCAT6 (Sport Concussion Assessment Tool), refer if red flags (neck pain, deteriorating consciousness, repeated vomiting, seizures, weakness). Graduated return-to-learn and return-to-sport protocols (symptom-limited activity, light aerobic exercise, sport-specific exercise, non-contact drills, full-contact practice, return to play — each stage about 24 hours minimum). Second impact syndrome can be fatal in young athletes.

topics.title: Sports Rehabilitation and Performance
topics.summary: Phases of rehabilitation, return-to-sport testing, tendinopathy, hamstring and ACL rehabilitation, and athlete support.

notes.b: Sports rehabilitation progresses through: acute/protection (control pain and swelling, protect healing tissue, maintain fitness of uninjured areas), restoration of range and early strength (isometric then isotonic), advanced strengthening and neuromuscular control (eccentric, plyometric, proprioceptive and agility training), sport-specific training, and return to sport (RTS) — ideally criteria-based rather than time-based. RTS criteria include full pain-free range, strength symmetry (limb symmetry index ≥ 90%), functional tests (hop tests — single hop, triple hop, crossover hop), psychological readiness (e.g. ACL-RSI scale), and sport-specific performance. Specific examples: hamstring strain (common in sprinters and footballers — progressive loading, eccentric Nordic exercises, high-speed running reintroduced gradually; recurrence is common), ACL reconstruction (about 9–12 months before return; neuromuscular training reduces re-injury), ankle sprain (balance and proprioception), and tendinopathy (patellar — 'jumper's knee', Achilles — progressive loading programmes: isometric, heavy slow resistance, energy storage).
k: Phases: protect → restore → strengthen → sport-specific → RTS

notes.b: Sports physiotherapists support performance and wellbeing: strength and conditioning collaboration, recovery strategies (sleep, nutrition, hydration, active recovery, massage, compression), taping and bracing, and education. Special populations: female athletes (relative energy deficiency in sport — RED-S, formerly the female athlete triad: low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, low bone density; higher ACL injury risk), young athletes (growth-related conditions — Osgood–Schlatter disease, Sever's disease; avoid early single-sport specialisation and overtraining), para-athletes (wheelchair shoulder problems, pressure care, autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injury — 'boosting' is banned), and masters athletes. Anti-doping: physiotherapists must know that athletes are responsible for any substance in their system (strict liability); check medications against the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Prohibited List; the Nigeria Anti-Doping Agency oversees compliance. Ethical issues include confidentiality, pressure to return injured players early, and conflicts between athlete welfare and team interests.
